Genesis.author: The book never names its author [[eob:Genesis]]. Until the 1600s Jews and Christians almost unanimously named Moses, and many still hold that view [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]] [[bo:18623]]. Many modern scholars see it as woven from older traditions, given its final shape by a priestly editor during or after the exile in Babylon [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]].
Genesis.date: If Moses wrote it, in the wilderness after the Exodus: about 1445 BC on the early dating [[bo:18623]], or by 1240 BC at the latest on the later one [[eob:Genesis]]. Scholars who see several sources place its final form during or after the exile [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]].
Genesis.to: The people of Israel, to help them understand their roots in Abraham, Isaac and Jacob [[bo:18623]], and as the groundwork for the rest of the books of Moses [[eob:Genesis]].
Genesis.why: The book never states its purpose [[eob:Genesis]]. It is a selective history that lays the foundation for the whole Bible [[bo:18623]]: creation, the spread of sin, and God’s promise to bless all nations through Abraham’s family [[bible:Genesis 12:1-3]].
Genesis.story: Chapters 1–11 tell the early history of humankind, and chapters 12–50 the story of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph [[eob:Genesis]]. God’s call of Abram begins a new history of blessing [[nabre:genesis/12]], and Paul says the promised offspring is Christ [[bible:Galatians 3:16]].
Genesis.genre: Narrative history, organised under ten headings, “these are the generations of…” (Hebrew toledot, best translated “history”) [[eob:Genesis]] [[bo:18623]].
Genesis.debate: How Genesis was written: the theory of J, E, D and P sources, and its critics [[eob:Genesis]] [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]]; and how its creation and flood accounts compare with other ancient Near Eastern stories, such as the Gilgamesh and Atrahasis epics [[nabre:genesis/6]] [[eob:Genesis]].
Genesis.structureNote: The book falls into two halves, the early history (1–11) and the story of the patriarchs (12–50) [[eob:Genesis]]; the outline below follows the main characters of the text.

Exodus.author: The book does not name its author [[eob:Book-Exodus]]. Very early Jewish tradition held that Moses wrote all of it, and many still hold that view [[eob:Book-Exodus]] [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]]. Many modern scholars see it as woven from older traditions; the worship chapters (25–31, 35–40) belong to the Priestly material [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]].
Exodus.date: The events: about 1446 BC on the early dating, or about 1260 BC on the late dating, which links the city of Raamses (1:11) with Pharaoh Rameses II; both are held by evangelical scholars [[ref:esv-exodus-date]]. The evidence is not enough for a final decision, but points to the second half of the second millennium BC [[eob:Book-Exodus]].
Exodus.to: The people of Israel, as the story of how God made them his own nation [[nabre:exodus/0]].
Exodus.why: It tells how God freed Israel from Egypt, bound them to himself in the covenant at Sinai, and came to dwell among them [[nabre:exodus/0]]. Its great themes are redemption, covenant, law and worship [[eob:Book-Exodus]].
Exodus.story: The name Exodus is Greek for “departure”; in Hebrew the book is called Shemoth, “Names”, from its opening words [[nabre:exodus/0]]. The rescue from Egypt is remembered every year at Passover [[bible:Exodus 12:14]], and the New Testament calls Christ “our Passover” [[bible:1 Corinthians 5:7]].
Exodus.genre: About half narrative, the first nineteen chapters, and about half law and instructions for worship [[eob:Book-Exodus]].
Exodus.debate: The date of the Exodus [[ref:esv-exodus-date]]; why no Egyptian king is named and why Egyptian monuments are silent, which is expected since defeats were not recorded [[eob:Book-Exodus]]; how its laws compare with Hammurabi’s code, with which direct parallels are fairly few [[eob:Book-Exodus]]; and how the book was composed from sources [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]].
Exodus.structureNote: The NABRE divides the book into eight parts [[nabre:exodus/0]]; the outline below follows them.

Leviticus.author: The book does not name its author [[eob:Leviticus]]. It presents its laws as given by God through Moses [[bible:Leviticus 26:46]], and some scholars defend that view [[eob:Leviticus]]. Many see it as part of the Priestly tradition (P), with signs of development within it [[nabre:leviticus/0]] [[eob:Leviticus]].
Leviticus.date: On the traditional view, the time at Sinai [[eob:Leviticus]]. Critical scholars date the Priestly material later, in its final form no later than about 550 BC on one view, or in the 400s BC on another [[eob:Leviticus]].
Leviticus.to: The people of Israel and their priests. Its laws are meant to shape the whole way of life of those who hear them [[nabre:leviticus/0]].
Leviticus.why: It sets out how the holy God can live among an unholy people [[eob:Leviticus]]: sacrifices, purity and holiness, the priesthood, the sanctuary and the feasts [[nabre:leviticus/0]].
Leviticus.story: It carries on the story of Exodus and stands at the centre of the five books of Moses [[nabre:leviticus/0]]. Its Hebrew name is its first word, “And he called” [[eob:Leviticus]]. Hebrews reads its priests and sacrifices as a shadow of Christ’s work [[eob:Leviticus]] [[bible:Hebrews 10:1]].
Leviticus.genre: Laws for worship and daily life, with a few short narratives [[nabre:leviticus/0]].
Leviticus.debate: How and when the book was composed from sources [[eob:Leviticus]]; what the verb kipper, “atone”, means: to wipe away, to cover, or to pay a ransom [[eob:Leviticus]]; and whether the Holiness laws came before or after Ezekiel, which cannot be shown with certainty [[eob:Leviticus]].
Leviticus.structureNote: The outline follows the five parts of the NABRE introduction [[nabre:leviticus/0]].

Numbers.author: Like the other books of the Pentateuch, it has traditionally been credited to Moses [[easton:Numbers-Book]]; it says Moses wrote down the list of Israel’s journeys [[bible:Numbers 33:2]]. Many modern scholars see it, like the rest of the Pentateuch, as woven from several traditions [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]].
Numbers.date: The events cover about thirty-eight years, from the second year after the Exodus to the fortieth [[easton:Numbers-Book]] [[nabre:numbers/0]]. Scholars who see several sources place the Pentateuch’s final form during or after the exile [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]].
Numbers.to: The people of Israel, who were about to enter the land God had promised [[nabre:numbers/0]].
Numbers.why: It follows two generations: the one that refused to trust God and died in the wilderness, and the new one being prepared to enter the land [[nabre:numbers/0]]. Its laws are set within the story [[nabre:numbers/0]].
Numbers.story: It continues the journey begun in Exodus [[nabre:numbers/0]]. The New Testament recalls its bronze serpent, Korah’s rebellion, Balaam’s prophecies and the water from the rock [[nabre:numbers/0]] [[bible:John 3:14-15]] [[bible:1 Corinthians 10:4]], and Hebrews uses the wilderness generation as a warning against unbelief [[bible:Hebrews 3:17-19]].
Numbers.genre: Law and history together, with two censuses, travel lists and the poetic oracles of Balaam [[nabre:numbers/0]].
structure: Rebellion and forty years in the wilderness
A new generation prepares to enter the land
Numbers.debate: How the book was composed [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]]; the route through the wilderness, since the list of stages is not complete and many places are not known [[nabre:numbers/33]]; and what exactly Moses’s sin at Meribah was, which the text does not make clear [[nabre:numbers/20]].
Numbers.structureNote: The NABRE divides the book into three parts [[nabre:numbers/0]]; the outline below follows them.

Deuteronomy.author: It is presented as three speeches of Moses [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]]. Those who hold that Moses wrote it point to its likeness to Hittite treaties of the second millennium BC [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]]; an editor completed it after his death [[bo:885]]. Others hold that it was written by an unknown author in the 600s BC, in King Josiah’s time [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]].
Deuteronomy.date: If by Moses, the 1300s or 1200s BC [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]], or about 1406 BC on the early dating of the Exodus [[bo:885]]. The NABRE judges it was probably composed over three centuries, from the 700s BC to after the exile [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]].
Deuteronomy.to: The new generation of Israel on the plains of Moab, about to enter the promised land [[nabre:deuteronomy/1]] [[tosn:Deuteronomy 4:13]].
Deuteronomy.why: To call Israel to choose between loving the LORD and keeping his commands, which brings blessing, or serving other gods, which brings curse [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]]: so that the nation might live and possess the land [[bo:885]].
Deuteronomy.story: Its language and ideas shape the books from Joshua to Kings [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]]. More than 80 Old Testament quotations in the New Testament come from it, and Jesus quoted it when tempted and when naming the greatest commandment [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]].
Deuteronomy.genre: Speeches of Moses that follow the pattern of an ancient covenant treaty, with laws, blessings and curses [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]] [[tosn:Deuteronomy 1:1]].
structure: Third address: covenant renewal and farewell
Deuteronomy.debate: Whether Moses wrote it or it was written in Josiah’s time [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]]; its relation to the book of the law found in the temple in 622 BC [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]]; and how closely it follows Hittite treaty forms [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]]. Its Greek name, “second law”, can mislead, since it is not a simple repeat of the law [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]].
Deuteronomy.structureNote: The NABRE divides the book into three addresses of Moses and the account of his death [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]]; the outline below follows them.

Joshua.author: The book does not say. The Talmud names Joshua, perhaps because he “wrote these words” of the covenant renewal (24:26) [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]] [[bible:Joshua 24:26]]. The NABRE treats it as part of the Deuteronomistic History, written for Israel late in the time of the kings [[nabre:joshua/0]].
Joshua.date: There are no clear markers, and scholars do not agree [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]]. A conservative view dates the writing between 1375 and 1045 BC; critical scholars suggest the 600s BC or the exile [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]].
Joshua.to: Israel, to show how the LORD gave them the land and how they might prosper in it [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]], and to warn them against losing it [[nabre:joshua/0]].
Joshua.why: To show Joshua following in Moses’s footsteps, the LORD giving the land, and the conditions for keeping it: trusting the LORD and staying united and faithful [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]] [[nabre:joshua/0]].
Joshua.story: God’s promise of the land is kept: “Nothing failed of any good thing which Yahweh had spoken” [[bible:Joshua 21:45]]. Joshua’s name means “the LORD saves”, the same name as Jesus [[nabre:numbers/13]].
Joshua.genre: History, the first of the books the Hebrew Bible calls the Former Prophets [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]], with lists of tribal lands that preserve older traditions [[nabre:joshua/0]].
Joshua.debate: When and by whom it was written [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]]; how its swift conquest fits Judges 1, which suggests a slow and piecemeal settlement [[nabre:joshua/0]]; and how to read the total destruction it describes, which the NABRE calls an idealisation, set against the New Testament command to love enemies [[nabre:joshua/0]].
Joshua.structureNote: The NABRE divides the book into three parts [[nabre:joshua/0]]; the outline below follows them, with the conquest in two halves.

Judges.author: Unknown. It was almost certainly not Samuel, as later tradition suggested; a later writer probably compiled it from older written sources [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].
Judges.date: The final editing reflects the early days of Israel’s kings [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]]. The period itself began about 1370–1360 BC on the early dating of the Exodus, or near the end of the 1200s BC on the later one [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].
Judges.to: Israel under its first kings, explaining why the tribes did not take all the land and pointing toward a king who would shepherd the people [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].
Judges.why: It shows an age that repeated itself without progress, defends God’s justice and patience when Israel kept disobeying, and supports the idea of a shepherd king [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].
Judges.story: A new generation falls into a cycle of rebellion and partial rescue [[tosn:Judges 2:10-19]]. It ends: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did that which was right in his own eyes” [[bible:Judges 21:25]], looking toward God’s covenant with David [[tosn:Judges 21:25]].
Judges.genre: Hero stories of twelve judges from different regions, framed by an introduction and two closing stories [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]] [[tosn:Judges 17:1-21:25]].
structure: Everyone did what was right in his own eyes
Judges.debate: How long the period of the judges lasted, which depends on the date of the Exodus [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]]; and whether the book argues for David’s rule rather than Saul’s, as some scholars think [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].
Judges.structureNote: The outline follows the book’s introduction, the stories of the judges and its two closing stories [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].

Ruth.author: Unknown [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]]. Since it closes with David’s family line, it was probably written after David began to reign, perhaps by someone close to him such as Samuel, Nathan or Abiathar [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].
Ruth.date: The events took place around 1100 BC, in the days of the judges [[tosn:Ruth 1:1]]. It was likely written after David became king [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].
Ruth.to: Israel, perhaps to show that David’s family was the chosen royal line, and to explain how a faithful Moabite woman became part of Israel [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].
Ruth.why: It shows God’s kindness reaching even those not born Israelites, and Ruth’s love for Naomi as a model of devotion [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].
Ruth.story: Ruth becomes King David’s great-grandmother [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]] [[bible:Ruth 4:17]], and she appears in Jesus’s family tree [[bible:Matthew 1:5]].
Ruth.genre: A short story that ends with a family line of ten generations, from Perez to David [[tosn:Ruth 4:18-22]].
Ruth.debate: When it was written, which affects what its purpose was [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].

1 Samuel.author: Unknown. It cannot have been Samuel alone, since his death is reported in 25:1 [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]]. Some suggest Samuel with the prophets Nathan and Gad (1 Chronicles 29:29), but the real author cannot be determined [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
1 Samuel.date: Its final form comes some time after Solomon’s death and the division of the kingdom in 930 BC [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
1 Samuel.to: Israel, about what kind of king fits God’s covenant [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
1 Samuel.why: Israel moves from judges to kings. Kingship as the people demanded it denied the covenant, Saul’s reign failed it, and David’s, though imperfect, truly reflected it [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
1 Samuel.story: Hannah’s song looks ahead to kingship in Israel and ultimately to Christ [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]]. God looks at the heart, not appearances [[bible:1 Samuel 16:7]].
1 Samuel.genre: Historical narrative with poetry, such as Hannah’s song (2:1–10) [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]]. 1 and 2 Samuel were one book until the Greek translators split them in two [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
1 Samuel.debate: Who wrote it, and how its mixed feelings about kingship fit together; the book resolves them in chapter 12 [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].

2 Samuel.author: Unknown. 1 and 2 Samuel were originally one book, and its real author cannot be determined [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
2 Samuel.date: David ruled the strongest kingdom of the region about 1000 BC [[tbd:004:David]]. The book reached its final form some time after the kingdom split in 930 BC [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
2 Samuel.to: Israel, about David’s reign and what kind of king fits God’s covenant [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
2 Samuel.why: David becomes king of all Israel, makes Jerusalem its centre, and receives God’s promise of a lasting dynasty [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]]; then his sin with Bathsheba brings trouble on his family [[bsn:2 Samuel 11:1–14:33]].
2 Samuel.story: God promises David a house that will last forever [[bible:2 Samuel 7:16]], a promise fulfilled in the eternal reign of Jesus Christ [[tosn:2 Samuel 7:19]].
2 Samuel.genre: Historical narrative with poetry, such as David’s laments and his song in chapter 22 [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]]. Chapters 21–24 are arranged by topic, not by time [[tosn:2 Samuel 21:1–24:25]].
2 Samuel.debate: Who wrote it and when it took its final form [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].

1 Kings.author: Unknown; the book is anonymous [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]. Jewish tradition in the Talmud names Jeremiah, and an origin among the prophets fits the evidence well [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]. It draws on official royal annals, “the chronicles of the kings” [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.date: The events run from Solomon’s accession to the divided kingdoms [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]; Solomon’s fourth year was about 967 BC [[tosn:1 Kings 6:1]] and the kingdom split under Rehoboam in 931 BC [[tosn:1 Kings 12:1]]. 1 and 2 Kings were completed in exile, likely between 561 and 539 BC [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.to: The exiles, who were asking how and why Jerusalem and the temple could fall [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.why: Solomon’s glory and temple, the split into Israel and Judah, and Elijah’s stand against Baal. The writer weighs this history by the standard of Deuteronomy [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.story: Each king is judged by faithfulness to God, not by political success [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]], and the book keeps showing words spoken by the prophets coming true [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.genre: History written for theological reasons, not a modern history textbook [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.debate: Who compiled it, and how the dates given for the kings of Israel and Judah fit together into one timeline [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].

2 Kings.author: Unknown; 1 and 2 Kings are anonymous [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]. Jewish tradition names Jeremiah, and an origin among the prophets fits the evidence well [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
2 Kings.date: It covers the divided kingdoms, the fall of Samaria in 722 BC [[tosn:2 Kings 17:5–6]], Jerusalem’s fall in 586 BC, and Jehoiachin’s release about 561 BC [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]. Written in exile, likely between 561 and 539 BC [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
2 Kings.to: The exiles, asking how and why the temple and David’s throne had fallen [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
2 Kings.why: Elisha’s miracles, the fall of Israel to Assyria and of Judah to Babylon, with a few faithful kings along the way. The writer measures the history by Deuteronomy [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
2 Kings.story: The exile is explained as the result of turning from God [[bible:2 Kings 17:7]]. It ends with Jehoiachin released, a hint that God would bring his people home [[tosn:2 Kings 25:27–30]].
2 Kings.genre: History written for theological reasons, drawing on royal annals [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
2 Kings.debate: How the reigns of the kings fit into one timeline, and how the book compares with Assyrian and Babylonian records [[tosn:2 Kings 17:5–6]] [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].

1 Chronicles.author: Unknown, usually called “the Chronicler” [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]]. The Talmud says Ezra wrote it, and many scholars agree, but there is no general agreement [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.date: Probably around 400 BC, in the Persian period [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.to: Jews living in Jerusalem under Persian rule after the exile [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.why: With David’s kingdom gone politically, the Chronicler finds the key to history in God’s covenant with David, and gives temple worship great weight [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.story: It retells Israel’s story from Adam to David. Chronicles tells of times David was faithful and leaves some of his failures to 2 Samuel [[bsn:1 Chronicles 9:35–20:8]].
1 Chronicles.genre: Genealogies (chapters 1–9) and the reign of David (chapters 10–29) [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.debate: Who wrote it and when, and whether the same author wrote Ezra and Nehemiah [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].

2 Chronicles.author: Unknown, usually called “the Chronicler”; the Talmud names Ezra, but there is no general agreement [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.date: Probably around 400 BC, in the Persian period [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.to: Jews in Jerusalem under Persian rule, for whom temple worship mattered greatly [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.why: Solomon’s reign, the kings of Judah, and an epilogue on the exile and return [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.story: It ends with Cyrus inviting God’s people to go up to Jerusalem [[bible:2 Chronicles 36:23]]. Chronicles stands at the very end of the Hebrew Bible [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.genre: History drawing on earlier records, retelling Samuel and Kings with its own concerns [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.debate: Who wrote it and when, and whether its author also wrote Ezra and Nehemiah [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].

Ezra.author: Many believe Ezra himself collected and wrote the material; parts are told in his own words [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]].
Ezra.date: The events run from Cyrus’s decree after he took Babylon in 539 BC to Ezra’s work under Artaxerxes I (465–424 BC) [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]]. Ezra came about 13 years before Nehemiah, who arrived in 445 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]].
Ezra.to: The Jews who returned from exile under Persian rule [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]].
Ezra.why: Exiles return from Babylon, rebuild the temple [[bible:Ezra 6:15]], and Ezra the scribe teaches God’s law [[bible:Ezra 7:10]].
Ezra.story: God moved a king who did not know him, Cyrus of Persia, to let his people go home [[tosn:Ezra 1:1]].
Ezra.genre: History with official letters written in Aramaic and a first-person account by Ezra [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]].
structure: The first return and the temple
Ezra.debate: Whether Ezra came before Nehemiah [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]], and how to understand the divorces of chapter 10, for which the law gave no clear instructions [[tosn:Ezra 10:4]].

Nehemiah.author: Nehemiah tells much of it in his own words [[bible:Nehemiah 1:1]]. Ezra and Nehemiah formed one book in the early Hebrew Bible [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]].
Nehemiah.date: Nehemiah came to Jerusalem in 445 BC, under Artaxerxes I [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]].
Nehemiah.to: The Jews who had returned to Judah under Persian rule [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]].
Nehemiah.why: Nehemiah, the Persian king’s cupbearer, rebuilds Jerusalem’s walls and leads the people to renew their covenant with God [[bible:Nehemiah 1:11]] [[bible:Nehemiah 10:29]].
Nehemiah.story: One of the last of the Jewish historical books [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]].
Nehemiah.genre: First-person memoir with lists and a covenant ceremony [[bible:Nehemiah 7:5]] [[bible:Nehemiah 9:38]].
Nehemiah.debate: The exact order of Ezra’s and Nehemiah’s work; the book’s message is clear either way [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]].

Esther.author: Unknown. Esther 9:20 says Mordecai “wrote these things”, which may mean he wrote part or all of it [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]].
Esther.date: Set under Xerxes, who died in 465 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]]. When it was written is uncertain: some say shortly after 465 BC, others much later [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]].
Esther.to: Jews living in the Persian empire, and to explain the feast of Purim [[bible:Esther 9:26-28]].
Esther.why: A Jewish queen of Persia risks her life to save her people from a plot to destroy them [[bible:Esther 4:16]].
Esther.story: God’s name never appears, perhaps because the book was meant for the official Persian court record [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]]; yet the reversals show God’s guiding hand [[tosn:Esther 7:9]].
Esther.genre: A court story written by someone who knew Persian court life well [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]].
Esther.debate: When and why it was written, and the extra passages in the Greek version [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]] [[tbd:005:Esther, Additions to]].

Psalms.author: Many writers. The Hebrew titles credit David with 73 psalms, Asaph with 12 and the sons of Korah with 11, Solomon with two, and Moses and Ethan with one each [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]]. The titles were added early and are a reasonably reliable guide [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.date: From David’s time, around 1000 BC [[tbd:004:David]], to after the exile [[tosn:Psalm 126:1–6]]. The collection was complete before the Greek translation at the end of the 200s BC [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.to: God’s people at worship, in every situation of life [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.why: Every emotion, from bitter complaint to joyful praise, brought into communion with God [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.story: The apostles use the Psalms to describe the life and work of Jesus the Messiah [[tosn:Psalm 1:1–6]]; most royal psalms are also messianic [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.genre: Poetry in five books (1–41, 42–72, 73–89, 90–106, 107–150), perhaps echoing the five books of Moses, each of the first four ending with a doxology [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.debate: What the titles mean: “of David” usually means by David, but with groups it may mean from their collection [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].

Job.author: Unknown; no one is named as author [[tbd:002:Book of Job]].
Job.date: Uncertain. Most modern scholars think it was written after the exile, around the 400s BC; others place it near the end of the exile, in Solomon’s time, or in the age of the patriarchs [[tbd:002:Book of Job]]. Job’s wealth in livestock fits the patriarchal era [[tbd:002:Book of Job]].
Job.to: Anyone asking why good people suffer [[tbd:002:Book of Job]].
Job.why: A good man loses everything [[bible:Job 1:13-19]], argues with friends who say he must deserve it [[bsn:Job 4:1–31:40]], and finally meets God in the whirlwind [[bible:Job 38:1]].
Job.story: God speaking from the whirlwind gives no explanation for why the righteous suffer; we learn to trust the Creator’s wisdom [[tbd:002:Book of Job]].
Job.genre: A prose prologue and epilogue around long poetic speeches [[tbd:002:Book of Job]] [[bsn:Job 4:1–31:40]].
Job.debate: Who wrote it and when, and whether it combines earlier writings [[tbd:002:Book of Job]].

Proverbs.author: Several writers, named in the book’s seven or more sections: Solomon (970–930 BC) for the main parts, “the wise”, Agur and King Lemuel [[tbd:016:Proverbs, Book of]]. Whether 1:1 means Solomon wrote chapters 1–9 is best left open [[tbd:016:Proverbs, Book of]].
Proverbs.date: Solomon’s reign, 970–930 BC, with more of his proverbs gathered by King Hezekiah’s men (728–686 BC) [[tosn:Proverbs 25:1–29:27]] [[tbd:016:Proverbs, Book of]].
Proverbs.to: Young people especially, “to give prudence to the simple, knowledge and discretion to the young man” [[bible:Proverbs 1:4]].
Proverbs.why: Practical wisdom for daily life, built on the fear of the Lord, which is stressed throughout [[tbd:016:Proverbs, Book of]].
Proverbs.story: Wisdom personified in chapter 8 is one of the Old Testament’s most remarkable pictures [[tbd:016:Proverbs, Book of]]; Christians see Jesus as the high point of God’s wisdom [[tosn:Proverbs 8:22–25]].
Proverbs.genre: Poems and two-line sayings, often in contrasting pairs [[tbd:016:Proverbs, Book of]]. They describe how life generally works under God, not guarantees [[tbd:016:Proverbs, Book of]].
structure: A father’s lessons and Lady Wisdom
Agur and Lemuel; the worthy woman
Proverbs.debate: Its close parallel with the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope in 22:17–23:11, and which came first [[tbd:016:Proverbs, Book of]].

Ecclesiastes.author: The Teacher, Qoheleth, “son of David, king in Jerusalem” [[bible:Ecclesiastes 1:1]]. Scholars disagree: some credit Solomon, others a later writer using Solomon’s figure [[tbd:002:Book of Ecclesiastes]].
Ecclesiastes.date: If Solomon, around 940 BC; most who deny this date it after the exile, some to the 400s and many to the 200s BC [[tbd:002:Book of Ecclesiastes]]. Fragments from the 100s BC were found at Qumran [[tbd:002:Book of Ecclesiastes]].
Ecclesiastes.why: It shows that a view of life which leaves God out is meaningless [[tbd:002:Book of Ecclesiastes]], and ends: fear God and keep his commandments [[bible:Ecclesiastes 12:13]].
Ecclesiastes.story: Honest wisdom about life’s limits: “vanity” is hebel, a breath or vapour [[tosn:Ecclesiastes 1:2]].
Ecclesiastes.genre: Reflections and sayings, with a closing note by an editor [[tosn:Ecclesiastes 12:9–14]].
structure: Youth, age and the end of the matter
Ecclesiastes.debate: Who wrote it and when [[tbd:002:Book of Ecclesiastes]].

Song of Solomon.author: The title can mean the song is by Solomon (970–930 BC) or dedicated to him; authorship cannot be known with certainty [[tbd:019:Song of Solomon]].
Song of Solomon.date: If by Solomon, the later 900s BC; otherwise later, but completed before 586 BC [[tbd:019:Song of Solomon]].
Song of Solomon.to: Israel; it may gather love poetry from different periods [[tbd:019:Song of Solomon]].
Song of Solomon.why: Love poetry between a woman and a man, celebrating faithful love and desire within marriage [[tosn:Song of Solomon 4:1–5:1]].
Song of Solomon.story: Jewish and Christian scholars long read it as an allegory, Christians of the love between Christ and the church [[tbd:019:Song of Solomon]].
Song of Solomon.genre: Love poetry, perhaps an anthology or dramatic poetry like Job [[tbd:019:Song of Solomon]].
structure: Beauty and the strength of love
Song of Solomon.debate: How to interpret it: allegory, drama, or a collection of love songs [[tbd:019:Song of Solomon]].

Isaiah.author: Isaiah son of Amoz of Jerusalem, whose ministry ran mainly from 740 to 700 BC [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]]. Many scholars assign chapters 40–66 to a “second” or “third” Isaiah, but the book also shows signs of unity: chapters 36–39 form a bridge between its halves, and “Holy One of Israel” appears 12 times in chapters 1–39 and 14 times in 40–66 [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]].
Isaiah.date: Chapters 1–39 were mostly written by about 700 BC; 37:38 mentions Sennacherib’s death in 681 BC, so some parts come from Isaiah’s later years [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]]. Chapters 40–66 address the exiles of about 550 BC [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]].
Isaiah.to: Judah in the Assyrian period, then the exiles in Babylon whom God promises to bring home [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]].
Isaiah.why: Because God is the Holy One of Israel he must punish sin, yet he graciously provides salvation; the Tyndale dictionary compares Isaiah’s place in the Old Testament to Romans in the New [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]].
Isaiah.story: Isaiah is usually regarded as the greatest of the writing prophets [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]]. The sign of Immanuel to King Ahaz (ch. 7), the servant of the Lord who is “a light for the Gentiles” (42:6) and Cyrus raised up to free the exiles are among its key moments [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]].
Isaiah.genre: Prophetic poetry of great literary beauty, with a historical section in chapters 36–39 [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]].
structure: The new heavens and new earth
Isaiah.debate: Whether the book has one author or several; the naming of Cyrus (539 BC) is a main reason its unity has been questioned [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]].

Jeremiah.author: Jeremiah, the prophet from Anathoth, wrote most of it; his secretary Baruch wrote down his messages and may have edited them [[tbd:002:Book of Jeremiah]]. Chapter 52 is an editorial addition, since Jeremiah’s own words end at 51:64 [[tbd:002:Book of Jeremiah]].
Jeremiah.date: During Jeremiah’s ministry, about 627 to 586 BC; he was later taken to Egypt, around 584 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Jeremiah]].
Jeremiah.to: Judah before and after Jerusalem fell, the captives in Babylon (ch. 29), and the Jews in Egypt [[tbd:002:Book of Jeremiah]].
Jeremiah.why: To “to uproot and to tear down… to build and to plant” (1:10): Jeremiah condemned sin, urged submission to God’s judgement through Babylon, and pointed to a new covenant written on the heart [[tbd:002:Book of Jeremiah]].
Jeremiah.story: The fall of Jerusalem seen from inside [[tbd:010:Jeremiah (Person)]]. The promise of a new covenant (31:31–34) is the longest New Testament quotation from Jeremiah (Hebrews 8:8–12) [[tbd:002:Book of Jeremiah]], and Jesus’ death began that covenant [[tosn:Jeremiah 31:34]].
Jeremiah.genre: Prophetic poetry and sermons, with history of Jeremiah’s sufferings and symbolic acts [[tbd:002:Book of Jeremiah]].
structure: Symbolic acts and sufferings before the siege
Jeremiah.debate: The order of the messages is not chronological and cannot be fully explained; the Greek Septuagint is about 2,700 words shorter and places chapters 46–51 after 25:13 [[tbd:002:Book of Jeremiah]].

Lamentations.author: Traditionally Jeremiah, as the Septuagint and Latin Vulgate say; many scholars question this because the style differs, but shared phrases such as “terrors on every side” and “wormwood” support it [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]]. The poems do not name their author [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]].
Lamentations.date: Shortly after Jerusalem fell in 586 BC; its vivid detail suggests an eyewitness [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]].
Lamentations.to: The Jews who had lived through the fall of Jerusalem, to give them words for their grief [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]].
Lamentations.why: To voice the grief of the whole people, to point them to God for comfort, and to explain the fall: the people’s sin, and God’s justice even toward his own [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]].
Lamentations.story: It shows lament as an act of faith: grief brought honestly to God, with hope at its centre in 3:22–23 [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]].
Lamentations.genre: Five poems forming a formal dirge; chapters 1–4 are acrostics on the Hebrew alphabet [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]].
Lamentations.debate: Whether Jeremiah wrote it, and why the poems use such complex alphabet patterns (perhaps to aid memory, or to express completeness) [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]].

Ezekiel.author: Ezekiel son of Buzi, of a priestly family, taken to Babylon with King Jehoiachin when he was about 25 [[tbd:005:Ezekiel, Book of]].
Ezekiel.date: His first vision came in 593 BC [[tosn:Ezekiel 1:2]]; the latest dated message is from the 27th year of exile, about 571 BC [[bible:Ezekiel 29:17]].
Ezekiel.to: The exiles settled at Tel-abib by the Kebar canal, who hoped for a quick return home [[tbd:005:Ezekiel, Book of]].
Ezekiel.why: To show why Jerusalem and its temple fell, and then to proclaim hope: a restored people, a new covenant, God’s Spirit and his glory returning [[tbd:005:Ezekiel, Book of]].
Ezekiel.story: God revealed himself in Babylon, against all expectations, showing he had not abandoned his people [[tbd:005:Ezekiel, Book of]]. The new heart (36:26) and the river of life (ch. 47) are taken up in the New Testament [[tosn:Ezekiel 36:16–38]] [[bible:Revelation 22:1-2]].
Ezekiel.genre: Visions, symbolic acts, parables and oracles, arranged by subject and by date [[tbd:005:Ezekiel, Book of]].
Ezekiel.debate: How chapters 34–48 are fulfilled beyond the return from exile: for Israel in the future, or in God’s work among all who share Abraham’s faith [[tbd:005:Ezekiel, Book of]]. The identity of Gog is also debated [[tosn:Ezekiel 38:1–39.29]].

Daniel.author: The book does not name its author. Jewish and Christian tradition held that Daniel wrote it all, and chapters 7–12 speak in his voice [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]].
Daniel.date: The stories run from about 605 BC to the early years of Cyrus, who took Babylon in 539 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]]. The conservative view dates the book to the 500s BC; another view dates it to about 165 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]].
Daniel.to: Jews living in exile under foreign rule, and later those suffering under Antiochus Epiphanes (175–163 BC) [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]].
Daniel.why: To explain history through faith: God controls history and guides it to a goal, giving hope to people in crisis [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]].
Daniel.story: Chapters 1–6 show how to stay faithful in a foreign land; chapters 7–12 show God’s rule over the empires [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]]. It contains one of the clearest Old Testament teachings on resurrection (12:2) [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]].
Daniel.genre: Stories and visions; in the Hebrew Bible it sits among the Writings, not the Prophets. Daniel 2:4–7:28 is in Aramaic [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]].
Daniel.debate: Its date (500s BC or about 165 BC), the identity of Darius the Mede, the four kingdoms, and the seventy sevens [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]] [[tosn:Daniel 9:24–27]].

Hosea.author: Hosea, whose ministry lasted at least 38 years, about 753 to 715 BC [[tbd:008:Hosea, Book of]].
Hosea.date: The late eighth century BC [[tbd:008:Hosea, Book of]].
Hosea.to: The northern kingdom of Israel in its last years; Hosea is the only writing prophet who lived and preached there [[tbd:008:Hosea, Book of]].
Hosea.why: To expose Israel’s unfaithfulness and urge them to return to God, showing through his own marriage God’s faithful, unbreakable love [[tbd:008:Hosea, Book of]].
Hosea.story: The first of the twelve shorter prophets [[tbd:008:Hosea, Book of]]. Matthew applies “out of Egypt I called my son” (11:1) to Jesus [[tosn:Hosea 11:1]].
Hosea.genre: Hosea’s marriage as a living sign, followed by prophecies mostly in the order given [[tosn:Hosea 4:1–14.9]] [[tbd:008:Hosea, Book of]].
structure: Love that will not let go
Hosea.debate: How to understand Hosea’s marriage to Gomer, and whether the passages about Judah and future blessing are original; most scholars accept the book’s unity [[tbd:008:Hosea, Book of]].

Joel.author: Joel son of Pethuel; Scripture tells us nothing more about either, and the name was common [[tbd:002:Book of Joel]].
Joel.date: Uncertain: some date it after Nehemiah rebuilt the walls (around 400 BC), others earlier [[tbd:002:Book of Joel]].
Joel.to: Judah and Jerusalem after a locust plague worse than any before [[tbd:002:Book of Joel]].
Joel.why: Joel saw the plague as a warning of the greater day of the Lord and promised restoration if the people returned to God with prayer and fasting [[tbd:002:Book of Joel]].
Joel.story: God promises to pour out his Spirit on all people, which Peter quotes at Pentecost [[bsn:Joel 2:28–3:21]] [[bible:Acts 2:16-21]].
Joel.genre: Prophetic poetry using the language of the day of the Lord [[bsn:Joel 2:28–3:21]].
structure: The locusts and a call to return
The Spirit and the day of Yahweh
Joel.debate: Its date, and whether the invaders of chapter 2 are locusts, a human army or future battles [[tbd:002:Book of Joel]] [[tosn:Joel 2:1–11]].

Amos.author: Amos, a herdsman and grower of fig trees from Tekoa, south of Jerusalem; there is no strong reason to think someone else wrote the book [[tbd:002:Book of Amos]].
Amos.date: Under Uzziah and Jeroboam II (792–740 BC), probably no later than about 760 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Amos]].
Amos.to: The prosperous northern kingdom of Israel; he preached mainly at Bethel [[tbd:002:Book of Amos]].
Amos.why: One of the Bible’s strongest warnings against injustice, oppression and religious hypocrisy [[tbd:002:Book of Amos]].
Amos.story: A farmer from Judah sent north to a nation richer than at any time since Solomon [[tbd:002:Book of Amos]]. God wanted justice to flow like water (5:24) [[tbd:002:Book of Amos]].
Amos.genre: Spoken oracles, five visions and a short story from Amos’s life (7:10–14) [[tbd:002:Book of Amos]].
structure: Judgement on the nations and Israel
Amos.debate: Whether the visions and oracles were joined later, and whether some passages were added; the evidence does not require it [[tbd:002:Book of Amos]].

Obadiah.author: Obadiah; we know almost nothing about him, not even his father’s name or home town [[tbd:002:Book of Obadiah]].
Obadiah.date: Probably just before or around the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Obadiah]].
Obadiah.to: Judah, with a message about Edom [[tbd:002:Book of Obadiah]].
Obadiah.why: To announce Edom’s fall for its cruelty to Judah, and to show that God is in control even when Judah has lost its power [[tbd:002:Book of Obadiah]].
Obadiah.story: Edom descended from Esau, Jacob’s brother, so its betrayal was a brother’s betrayal [[tosn:Obadiah 1:6]]. The remnant of Judah would survive and Zion be restored [[tbd:002:Book of Obadiah]].
Obadiah.debate: Its exact date, and its shared wording with Jeremiah 49:7–22 [[tosn:Obadiah 1:2–4]] [[tosn:Jeremiah 49:7–22]].

Jonah.author: Traditionally Jonah son of Amittai, a prophet under Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25); some think another author wrote it later [[tbd:002:Book of Jonah]].
Jonah.date: If by Jonah, during Jeroboam II’s reign (793–753 BC); others date it after Nineveh’s fall or after the exile [[tbd:002:Book of Jonah]].
Jonah.to: God’s people, who needed to learn that his mercy reaches even their enemies [[tbd:002:Book of Jonah]].
Jonah.why: Jonah ran because he knew Nineveh would repent and did not want God’s mercy shown to the hated Assyrians [[tbd:002:Book of Jonah]].
Jonah.story: Jesus used Jonah’s three days in the fish as a sign of his death and resurrection, and Nineveh’s repentance as a rebuke to his own generation [[tbd:002:Book of Jonah]].
Jonah.genre: A story rather than a collection of prophecies, with a psalm-like prayer in chapter 2 [[tbd:002:Book of Jonah]] [[tosn:Jonah 2:1–9]].
Jonah.debate: Whether it is history or a parable; many scholars have defended its historical accuracy [[tbd:002:Book of Jonah]].

Micah.author: Micah of Moresheth, a frontier town near Gath; he is named only in Micah 1:1 and Jeremiah 26:18 [[tbd:002:Book of Micah]].
Micah.date: Under Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (about 750–686 BC), though probably not that whole time; some messages come before Samaria fell in 722 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Micah]].
Micah.to: Everyone, but especially Jerusalem and Samaria, land-grabbers, false prophets, judges, priests and dishonest merchants [[tbd:002:Book of Micah]].
Micah.why: Judgement is coming, and the answer to sin is “to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” (6:8), possible because God forgives [[tbd:002:Book of Micah]].
Micah.story: It names Bethlehem as the birthplace of a ruler greater than David, quoted in Matthew 2 [[tosn:Micah 5:2]].
Micah.genre: About 20 separate messages of judgement and hope [[tbd:002:Book of Micah]].
Micah.debate: Its many sections may come from different times, so it is hard to state a single message [[tbd:002:Book of Micah]].

Nahum.author: Nahum the Elkoshite; Elkosh is probably an unknown town, perhaps Elcesi in Judah [[tbd:002:Book of Nahum]].
Nahum.date: Probably the mid-600s BC, after Thebes fell (about 663 BC) and while Assyria still dominated Judah [[tbd:002:Book of Nahum]].
Nahum.to: Judah under Assyrian domination [[tbd:002:Book of Nahum]].
Nahum.why: To announce the fall of Nineveh and show God’s power in history, his care for those who trust him (1:7) and his promise to end Assyria’s oppression (1:13) [[tbd:002:Book of Nahum]].
Nahum.story: Nineveh, spared in Jonah’s time, returned to cruelty and fell in 612 BC [[tosn:Nahum 3:19]] [[tbd:002:Book of Nahum]].
Nahum.genre: A long poem about the fall of a city [[tbd:002:Book of Nahum]].
Nahum.debate: Its date: some place it close to 612 BC, and scholars who doubt prophecy date it after Nineveh’s fall [[tbd:002:Book of Nahum]].

Habakkuk.author: Habakkuk the prophet; we know very little about him beyond this book, and the musical notes in chapter 3 suggest he may have been a Levite [[tbd:002:Book of Habakkuk]].
Habakkuk.date: Probably begun between 612 and 605 BC and continued under King Jehoiakim (609–598 BC) [[tbd:002:Book of Habakkuk]].
Habakkuk.to: Judah in one of the hardest periods of its history, after Josiah’s death [[tbd:002:Book of Habakkuk]].
Habakkuk.why: To show that evil does not win forever: God rules history rightly, and the faithful see his work through faith [[tbd:002:Book of Habakkuk]].
Habakkuk.story: “The righteous will live by his faith” (2:4) became central to Paul’s teaching and to the Protestant Reformation [[tbd:002:Book of Habakkuk]].
Habakkuk.genre: A dialogue with God, five woes and a closing psalm-prayer [[tbd:002:Book of Habakkuk]].
Habakkuk.debate: Its exact date, and whether 2:4 means faith or faithfulness; the Hebrew ’emunah carries both steadfastness and trust [[tosn:Habakkuk 2:4]].

Zephaniah.author: Zephaniah, whose name means “he whom the Lord protects or hides”; his family line is unusually long, and some think his great-great-grandfather was King Hezekiah [[tbd:002:Book of Zephaniah]].
Zephaniah.date: Under King Josiah (640–609 BC), likely around 630 BC, before Nineveh fell in 612 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Zephaniah]].
Zephaniah.to: Judah, still marked by the idolatry of Manasseh’s reign [[tbd:002:Book of Zephaniah]].
Zephaniah.why: To condemn Judah’s religious sins and corrupt leaders and to warn of the day of the Lord, while promising that God would restore the faithful [[tbd:002:Book of Zephaniah]].
Zephaniah.story: Its warnings came true when Judah fell in 586 BC, which gives later readers reason to trust its promises of restoration [[tbd:002:Book of Zephaniah]].
Zephaniah.genre: Prophetic poetry centred on the day of the Lord [[tbd:002:Book of Zephaniah]].
Zephaniah.debate: Whether Scythian invasions, described by Herodotus, lie behind the book; there is no solid evidence [[tbd:002:Book of Zephaniah]].

Haggai.author: Haggai, one of the Jewish settlers in Jerusalem (Ezra 5:1–2; 6:14); he repeatedly states that God spoke to him [[tbd:008:Haggai, Book of]].
Haggai.to: Zerubbabel the governor, Joshua the high priest and the people who had returned from exile [[tbd:008:Haggai, Book of]].
Haggai.why: To correct the settlers for neglecting God’s house and encourage them in their troubles: today’s appearances do not predict what God will do tomorrow [[tbd:008:Haggai, Book of]].
Haggai.story: Its four dated messages got the temple rebuilt [[bible:Ezra 5:1-2]]. The greater glory of this house may point to the Messiah, who was presented and taught in the temple [[tosn:Haggai 2:9]].
Haggai.genre: Four dated prophetic messages [[tbd:008:Haggai, Book of]].
Haggai.debate: What the promise to Zerubbabel as God’s signet ring meant, since he soon disappears from the biblical record [[tosn:Haggai 2:21]].

Zechariah.author: Zechariah son of Berechiah; his name likely means “the Lord remembers” [[tbd:026:Zechariah, Book of]]. Chapters 9–14 do not name him, and most scholars place them later in his ministry [[tosn:Zechariah 9:1–14.21]].
Zechariah.date: Chapters 1–8 date from 520 to 518 BC; chapters 9–14 carry no dates [[tbd:026:Zechariah, Book of]].
Zechariah.to: The returned exiles, who had not yet rebuilt the temple [[tbd:026:Zechariah, Book of]].
Zechariah.why: To reassure and encourage: the temple would be rebuilt, and God’s kingdom would one day come in full. Its messages are repentance, eight night visions and the coming kingdom [[tbd:026:Zechariah, Book of]].
Zechariah.story: The longest of the minor prophets [[tbd:026:Zechariah, Book of]]. The Gospel accounts of Jesus’ suffering quote Zechariah 9–14 more than any other part of the prophets, and it shaped Revelation more than any other Old Testament book [[tbd:026:Zechariah, Book of]].
Zechariah.genre: Visions explained by an angel, oracles, and in chapters 9–12 apocalyptic writing [[tbd:026:Zechariah, Book of]].
Zechariah.debate: When chapters 9–14 were written, and how to interpret the shepherd passages; dating them is only a guess [[tbd:026:Zechariah, Book of]].

Malachi.author: Malachi, a name meaning “my messenger”; since the word appears in 3:1, some think it is a title rather than a name [[tbd:013:Malachi, Book of]].
Malachi.date: Probably just after 433 BC, when Nehemiah returned to Persia; Malachi addresses the same sins as Nehemiah 13 [[tbd:013:Malachi, Book of]].
Malachi.to: The people and priests of Judah after the return from exile, who doubted God’s love and justice [[tbd:013:Malachi, Book of]].
Malachi.why: To warn Judah to stop treating God lightly and repent, before the day of the Lord announced by God’s messenger [[tbd:013:Malachi, Book of]].
Malachi.story: The last book of the Old Testament [[tbd:013:Malachi, Book of]]. John the Baptist came “in the spirit and power of Elijah” to prepare the way for Jesus [[tbd:013:Malachi, Book of]].
Malachi.genre: Sermons in the form of disputations: God states a truth, the people object, God answers [[tosn:Malachi 1:2–5]].
Malachi.debate: Whether Malachi is a personal name or a title; an ancient tradition identified the messenger with Ezra [[tbd:013:Malachi, Book of]].

Matthew.author: Traditionally Matthew (Levi), the tax collector who became an apostle; the Gospel itself is anonymous.
Matthew.date: Most scholars: AD 70–90. Some: the 50s or 60s.
Matthew.to: Jewish Christians, showing Jesus as the promised Messiah.
Matthew.why: The life and teaching of Jesus, showing that he fulfils the Old Testament and teaches with God’s authority.
Matthew.story: The first book of the New Testament and the bridge from the Old. It opens with Jesus’s family tree back to Abraham and ends with the command to make disciples of all nations.
Matthew.genre: Ancient biography (a Gospel), built around five great blocks of teaching.
Matthew.debate: Its relationship to Mark and Luke (the “Synoptic problem”), and early reports that Matthew first wrote in Hebrew or Aramaic.

Mark.author: Traditionally John Mark, recording Peter’s preaching; the Gospel is anonymous.
Mark.date: Most scholars: about AD 65–70, the earliest Gospel.
Mark.to: Probably Christians in Rome facing persecution.
Mark.why: A fast-moving account of Jesus’s actions and his road to the cross, asking: who is this man?
Mark.story: Probably the first Gospel written; Matthew and Luke seem to have used it.
Mark.genre: Ancient biography; vivid, urgent, full of the word “immediately”.
Mark.debate: Why the earliest manuscripts end at 16:8, and the “messianic secret”: why Jesus tells people to keep quiet.

Luke.author: Luke, a doctor and companion of Paul; he also wrote Acts.
Luke.to: Theophilus, and a wider Gentile audience.
Luke.why: An orderly account of Jesus’s life, with special care for the poor, women, outsiders and prayer.
Luke.story: The first half of a two-volume work; Acts continues the story from Jerusalem to Rome.
Luke.genre: Ancient biography written with a historian’s preface.
Luke.debate: Its sources, and how its census under Quirinius fits Roman records.

John.author: Traditionally John the apostle, “the disciple whom Jesus loved”.
John.to: Believers and seekers: “that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ.”
John.why: Seven signs and long conversations reveal Jesus as the Word made flesh, the Son sent from the Father.
John.story: The most reflective Gospel, with the “I am” sayings and the deepest teaching on the Father, Son and Spirit.
John.genre: Ancient biography arranged around signs and discourses.
structure: The last evening with the disciples
John.debate: Who the beloved disciple is, how John relates to the other three Gospels, and the story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11), missing from the oldest copies.

Acts.author: Luke.
Acts.why: The risen Jesus sends the Spirit, and his followers carry the good news from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria and Rome.
Acts.story: The story of the first church, the bridge between the Gospels and the letters. Paul’s journeys give the setting for many of his letters.
Acts.genre: Ancient history with speeches and travel narratives (some in the first person: “we”).
structure: Paul’s first journey and the council
Paul’s trials and voyage to Rome
Acts.debate: How its picture of Paul fits Paul’s letters, and whether its speeches are summaries or Luke’s compositions.

Romans.author: Paul.
Romans.to: The church in Rome, Jews and Gentiles, which Paul had not yet visited.
Romans.why: Paul’s fullest explanation of the good news: all have sinned, and God makes people right with himself as a gift through faith in Christ.
Romans.story: The most influential letter in church history, central to Augustine, Luther and Wesley.
Romans.genre: A letter with a long theological argument.
structure: New life in Christ and the Spirit
Romans.debate: What Paul means by “the righteousness of God” and “works of the law” (the “New Perspective on Paul” debate).

1 Corinthians.author: Paul.
1 Corinthians.to: The church in Corinth, a busy and divided Greek port city.
1 Corinthians.why: Paul answers questions and problems: divisions, sexual ethics, food offered to idols, worship, spiritual gifts and the resurrection.
1 Corinthians.story: Contains the great chapter on love (13) and the earliest written account of the resurrection appearances (15).
1 Corinthians.genre: A pastoral letter answering a letter from the church.
structure: Divisions and the wisdom of the cross
1 Corinthians.debate: Head coverings and women speaking in church (11 and 14), and what “speaking in tongues” was.

2 Corinthians.author: Paul.
2 Corinthians.to: The church in Corinth after painful conflict.
2 Corinthians.why: Paul’s most personal letter: strength in weakness, the ministry of reconciliation, generosity, and a defence against rivals.
2 Corinthians.story: It shows the cost of ministry and the treasure “in clay vessels”.
2 Corinthians.debate: Whether chapters 10–13 were a separate letter, and the identity of the “super-apostles”.

Galatians.author: Paul.
Galatians.why: A passionate defence of freedom in Christ: Gentiles are part of God’s people by faith, not by circumcision and the law.
Galatians.story: Sometimes called the charter of Christian freedom; it lists the fruit of the Spirit.
structure: Faith and the promise to Abraham
Galatians.debate: Whether it was written to north or south Galatia, and its timing relative to the Jerusalem council in Acts 15.

Ephesians.author: Paul; some scholars think a follower wrote in his name.
Ephesians.to: Probably a circular letter to churches around Ephesus.
Ephesians.why: God’s plan to unite all things in Christ, Jews and Gentiles as one body, and how that new life looks at home and in the world.
Ephesians.story: A high view of the church and of grace: “by grace you have been saved through faith.”
Ephesians.genre: Letter: praise and teaching, then practical instruction.

Philippians.author: Paul, with Timothy.
Philippians.to: The church in Philippi, Paul’s close friends and supporters.
Philippians.why: A warm letter of thanks and joy, centred on Christ who humbled himself and was exalted.
Philippians.story: Contains the Christ hymn (2:6–11), perhaps one of the earliest Christian songs.
Philippians.debate: Where Paul was imprisoned (Rome, Ephesus or Caesarea).

Colossians.author: Paul, with Timothy; some scholars think a follower.
Colossians.to: The church in Colossae, which Paul had not visited.
Colossians.why: Christ is supreme over all creation and powers, so believers need nothing added to him.
Colossians.story: Its poem of Christ as the image of the invisible God (1:15–20) is a key text for the church’s understanding of who Jesus is.
Colossians.debate: The nature of the “Colossian heresy” and authorship.

1 Thessalonians.author: Paul, with Silas and Timothy.
1 Thessalonians.date: About AD 50, perhaps the earliest New Testament book.
1 Thessalonians.to: A young church in Thessalonica facing persecution.
1 Thessalonians.why: Encouragement for new believers, and comfort about those who have died before Jesus returns.
1 Thessalonians.story: Probably the oldest Christian writing we have.
structure: Living to please God and the Lord’s coming
1 Thessalonians.debate: What 4:13–18 teaches about the end, including the idea of a “rapture”.

2 Thessalonians.author: Paul; some scholars question it.
2 Thessalonians.to: The same church, confused about the end.
2 Thessalonians.why: The day of the Lord has not yet come; keep working and stand firm.
2 Thessalonians.story: A short follow-up to the first letter.
2 Thessalonians.debate: Authorship and the identity of “the restrainer”.

1 Timothy.author: Paul; many scholars think a later follower.
1 Timothy.to: Timothy, Paul’s co-worker leading the church in Ephesus.
1 Timothy.why: Guidance on sound teaching, prayer, church leaders, widows and money.
1 Timothy.story: One of the three “Pastoral Letters” about caring for churches.
1 Timothy.genre: Letter of instruction to a church leader.

2 Timothy.author: Paul.
2 Timothy.date: About AD 64–67, from prison in Rome near the end of his life.
2 Timothy.why: Paul’s last letter: guard the gospel, endure hardship, and preach the word.
2 Timothy.story: Paul’s farewell: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course.”
2 Timothy.debate: Authorship, though its personal details persuade many it is Paul’s.

Titus.author: Paul.
Titus.why: Appoint good leaders and teach a way of life that fits God’s grace.
Titus.story: Its summaries of grace (2:11–14; 3:4–7) are among the clearest in the New Testament.
Titus.debate: Authorship, with the other Pastoral Letters.

Philemon.author: Paul.
Philemon.to: Philemon, a church host in Colossae.
Philemon.why: Paul appeals for Onesimus, a runaway slave who became a Christian, to be welcomed back as a brother.
Philemon.story: A small letter about how the gospel changes relationships.
Philemon.debate: What Paul is asking Philemon to do, and what the letter implies about slavery.

Hebrews.author: Unknown; suggestions include Apollos, Barnabas and Priscilla.
Hebrews.to: Jewish Christians tempted to turn back.
Hebrews.why: Jesus is greater than angels, Moses and the priesthood; his sacrifice is once for all. Hold on in faith.
Hebrews.story: The great explanation of how the Old Testament’s priests, sacrifices and covenant point to Christ.
Hebrews.genre: A sermon sent as a letter: “a word of exhortation”.
structure: The new covenant and one sacrifice
Hebrews.debate: Who wrote it, and the warning passages (6:4–6) about falling away.

James.author: James, the brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem church.
James.to: “the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion”: Jewish Christians scattered abroad.
James.why: Practical wisdom: faith shows itself in action, in controlling the tongue and caring for the poor.
James.story: The New Testament’s book of wisdom, echoing the Sermon on the Mount.
James.genre: A letter of wisdom sayings and short sermons.
structure: The tongue and wisdom from above
James.debate: How 2:24 fits with Paul on faith; Luther called it “a letter of straw”, though most readers see the two as complementary.

1 Peter.author: Peter, with Silvanus’s help.
1 Peter.to: Christians scattered across Asia Minor facing hostility.
1 Peter.why: Hope for suffering believers: you are God’s people, so live well among outsiders and follow Christ’s example.
1 Peter.story: It applies Israel’s titles to the church: “a royal priesthood, a holy nation.”
1 Peter.debate: Authorship, and the meaning of Christ preaching to “the spirits in prison” (3:19).

2 Peter.author: Peter; many scholars think a later follower.
2 Peter.why: Grow in godliness, trust Scripture, and do not doubt the Lord’s return.
2 Peter.story: It mentions Paul’s letters as Scripture.
2 Peter.debate: Authorship, and its close relationship to Jude.

1 John.author: Traditionally John the apostle.
1 John.to: Churches unsettled by teachers who had left.
1 John.why: How to know you belong to God: walking in the light, loving one another, and believing that Jesus came in the flesh.
1 John.story: “God is love” (4:8) is one of the Bible’s simplest summaries.
1 John.debate: Who the opponents were, and the late added words in 5:7–8.

2 John.author: “The elder”, traditionally John.
2 John.to: “The chosen lady and her children”, probably a church.
2 John.why: Walk in love and truth, and do not welcome deceivers.
2 John.debate: Whether the lady is a person or a church.

3 John.author: “The elder”, traditionally John.
3 John.why: Praise for Gaius’s hospitality, and a warning about Diotrephes, a controlling leader.
3 John.story: A glimpse of everyday life in an early house church.
3 John.debate: The relationship between the elder and Diotrephes.

Jude.author: Jude, brother of James and of Jesus.
Jude.why: Contend for the faith, and stay in God’s love; it ends with a famous blessing.
Jude.story: It quotes the Jewish book of Enoch.
Jude.debate: Its use of books outside the Old Testament.

Revelation.author: John, exiled on Patmos; traditionally the apostle.
Revelation.date: About AD 95, under Domitian (some say about AD 68).
Revelation.why: Visions that pull back the curtain: the Lamb who was slain reigns, evil will be judged, and God will make all things new.
Revelation.story: The last book of the Bible. It gathers images from the whole Old Testament and ends where Genesis began: a garden, a river and the tree of life, now in a city.
Revelation.genre: Apocalypse, prophecy and letter, full of symbols and numbers.
structure: The risen Christ and letters to seven churches
The end and the new creation
Revelation.debate: How to read it: as about the first century (preterist), church history (historicist), the end times (futurist) or timeless symbols (idealist); and the millennium in chapter 20.
